facts.statement: Mekosuchus is an extinct genus of crocodilian from Australasia.
facts.quote: Mekosuchus is a genus of extinct Australasian mekosuchine crocodilian.

facts.statement: Species of Mekosuchus were generally small, terrestrial animals under 2 meters long with short, blunt snouts and strong limbs.
facts.quote: Species of Mekosuchus were generally small-sized (less than 2 m long), terrestrial animals with short, blunt-snouted heads and strong limbs.

facts.statement: M. inexpectatus possessed bulbous rear teeth that may have been adapted for cracking the shells of crustaceans and molluscs.
facts.quote: M. inexpectatus is known to have had bulbous posterior teeth that may have been used to crack the shells of crustaceans and molluscs.

facts.statement: Some researchers suggest that Mekosuchus species were possibly nocturnal and lived near rainforest streams.
facts.quote: Some researchers suggest that they were possibly nocturnal animals living in close association with rainforest streams.

facts.statement: The first fossil bone of Mekosuchus, a fragmentary quadratojugal, was collected from Kanumera Bay in New Caledonia in 1981.
facts.quote: Fossils of Mekosuchus were initially recovered from various different sites across New Caledonia, with the first bone, a fragmentary quadratojugal, being collected from Kanumera Bay in 1981.

facts.statement: Mekosuchus fossils were first reported by Eric Buffetaut in 1983 and formally described by Balouet and Buffetaut in 1987.
facts.quote: Such fossils were first reported by Eric Buffetaut in 1983 and properly described by him and Jean-Christophe Balouet four years later in 1987.

facts.statement: The species M. whitehunterensis was described by Paul Willis in 1997 from fossils found at the Riversleigh World Heritage Area in Queensland.
facts.quote: Ten years later, in 1997, a second species was described by Paul Willis from the Riversleigh World Heritage Area in Queensland.

facts.statement: The species M. kalpokasi was named in 2002 based on fragmentary remains found at an archaeological site on Vanuatu.
facts.quote: The most recently described species is Mekosuchus kalpokasi, which was named in 2002 from fragmentary remains discovered at an archaeological site on Vanuatu.

facts.statement: Researchers initially classified Mekosuchus as an early eusuchian and placed it in its own family, Mekosuchidae, due to its unique anatomy.
facts.quote: Due to the strange anatomy of the material, they initially assumed the animal represented an early eusuchian (at the time considered a suborder of Crocodylia) and placed it in its own family, the Mekosuchidae.

facts.statement: Mekosuchus fossils range from the Oligocene to the Holocene, with survival until approximately 1,700 years ago being possible but unconfirmed.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Oligocene – Holocene, Survival until just 1,700 years ago is possible, but not certain.

facts.statement: Mekosuchus likely went extinct around 3,000 years ago during the Holocene, though some authors suggest they may have survived more recently.
facts.quote: Mekosuchus possibly died out approximately 3,000 years ago, during the Holocene, but some authors have also suggested that they may have survived until even more recently.

facts.statement: The earliest members of Mekosuchus lived during the Oligocene and Miocene on mainland Australia.
facts.quote: Mekosuchus was a successful and widespread genus, with its earliest members being found during the Oligocene and Miocene in mainland Australia.

facts.statement: Radiocarbon dating suggests M. inexpectatus fossils from the Isle of Pines date to roughly 3,750 years before present.
facts.quote: M. inexpectatus, from the Holocene of New Caledonia. Radiocarbon dating suggests that the M. inexpectatus fossils from the Isle of Pines date to roughly 3,750 years BP.

facts.statement: M. kalpokasi lived on the island of Éfaté in Vanuatu approximately 3,200 to 2,706 years before present.
facts.quote: M. kalpokasi, which lived on the island of Éfaté of Vanuatu approximately 3,200 to 2,706 years BP.

facts.statement: M. sanderi lived during the Early Miocene on the Australian mainland in what is now Queensland.
facts.quote: M. sanderi is one of two Mekosuchus species known from the mainland of Australia, and lived during the Early Miocene in what is now Queensland.

facts.statement: M. whitehunterensis is the oldest known species of Mekosuchus, living during the late Oligocene and early Miocene in Queensland.
facts.quote: M. whitehunterensis is the oldest known species and lived during the late Oligocene and early Miocene in Queensland.

facts.statement: The cause of Mekosuchus extinction is debated; while some suggest human involvement, others note insufficient evidence of overlap with human settlements and lack of direct signs of human impact.
facts.quote: What caused their extinction is unclear. Although some researchers suggest a human cause, others point out that the potential overlap with human settlements is insufficiently understood and no direct signs of human involvement have been found.

facts.statement: Due to poor preservation and overlapping ranges, some researchers suggest M. kalpokasi may be synonymous with M. inexpectatus.
facts.quote: For this reason, the poor preservation of the same area in the type species and the two species geographic and temporal range, Holt and colleagues suggest that this species may be synonymous with M. inexpectatus.

facts.statement: The name Mekosuchus combines the Drehu word 'Mek' for Grande Terre with the Greek suffix '-suchus' meaning crocodile.
facts.quote: The generic name of Mekosuchus derives from the Drehu name for Grande Terre, Mek, in combination with the suffix -suchus meaning crocodile.

facts.statement: Four species of Mekosuchus are currently recognized, all known primarily from fragmentary fossil remains.
facts.quote: Four species are currently recognized, M. inexpectatus, M. whitehunterensis, M. sanderi and M. kalpokasi, all known primarily from fragmentary remains.

facts.statement: Mekosuchus had a short and raised skull shape that differed from the elongated and flattened skulls of most modern crocodiles.
facts.quote: The skull of Mekosuchus was brachycephalic or altirostral, meaning that it was notably short and raised rather than elongated and flattened as seen in most extant crocodilian species.

facts.statement: Mekosuchus possessed large eye sockets that were uniquely formed partly by the maxilla bone, a feature not found in other crocodilians.
facts.quote: The eye sockets were well-developed and large and, unique among crocodilians, are in part formed by the maxilla, preventing the jugal and lacrimal bone from contacting each other.

facts.statement: Mekosuchus displayed a wave-like arrangement of teeth in its jaw known as festooning.
facts.quote: The tooth row of Mekosuchus is placed in a distinct, wave-like manner also referred to as festooning.

facts.statement: Mekosuchus is characterized by a nearly closed lower jaw opening and out-turned flanges on specific jaw bones.
facts.quote: The mandibular fenestra is strongly reduced, being almost closed in M. whitehunterensis, and the angular and surangular bones possess out-turned flanges, both of these are diagnostic for Mekosuchus.

facts.statement: The neck vertebrae of M. whitehunterensis were shorter than those of the modern freshwater crocodile, despite the animal's small overall size.
facts.quote: The vertebrae of M. whitehunterensis are described in greater detail. They are procoelous and the neck (cervical) vertebrae specifically were noted to be shorter than those of the extant freshwater crocodile, even when accounting for the small size of Mekosuchus.

facts.statement: Despite its small size, Mekosuchus likely possessed very strong neck muscles based on its vertebrae structure.
facts.quote: This has been taken as evidence that, in spite of being small, Mekosuchus had well developed and strong epaxial neck musculature.

facts.statement: Mekosuchus species possessed bony armor plates known as osteoderms, particularly on the back and tail of mainland species.
facts.quote: Various parts of the osteoderms, the bony armor, are known from across the different species and were specifically mentioned for M. inexpectatus and the Oligocene mainland species.

facts.statement: The oldest Mekosuchus species had blade-like teeth with flattened sides designed for slicing.
facts.quote: The oldest species, M. whitehunterensis, was described as having smooth maxillary teeth that would display flattened sides towards the back of the jaw, making them blade-like.

facts.statement: M. inexpectatus had bulbous, molar-like teeth at the back of its jaw that were adapted for crushing rather than slicing.
facts.quote: The teeth of M. inexpectatus are better known, but likewise fail to display the same condition as seen in the continental species. Rather than being blade-like, the posterior teeth of M. inexpectatus were bulbous molariforms, better suited for crushing than for slicing.

facts.statement: Both M. inexpectatus and M. whitehunterensis exhibited a full overbite where upper teeth overlapped lower teeth.
facts.quote: M. inexpectatus displays a full overbite in the maxillary toothrow and the same is the case for M. whitehunterensis.

facts.statement: M. sanderi and M. kalpokasi had a mixed dentition pattern combining an overbite with interlocking teeth between specific upper and lower jaw positions.
facts.quote: M. sanderi and M. kalpokasi on the other hand feature a mix. In both of these species, the teeth towards the tip of the jaw and towards the back were arranged in an overbite, however, M. sanderi had an interlocking dentary tooth between the 7th and 8th teeth of the maxilla, while in M. kalpokasi the dentition interlocked between the 6th and 7th as well as the 7th and 8th maxillary teeth.

facts.statement: In 2007, researchers reconstructed the skull of M. inexpectatus as resembling modern dwarf crocodiles after finding new fossil remains.
facts.quote: Following the discovery of additional remains, Holt and colleagues reconstructed Mekosuchus inexpectatus in 2007 with a skull similar to that of modern dwarf crocodiles.

facts.statement: In 2014, a reconstruction of the M. whitehunterensis skull was produced showing a gently sloping snout that differed significantly from earlier views of the genus.
facts.quote: In 2014 on the other hand, Scanlon produced a composite skeletal for the skull of M. whitehunterensis, reconstructing it with a much more gently sloping rostrum that differed greatly from the previous depiction of the genus.

facts.statement: There is significant disagreement among researchers regarding the exact shape of the Mekosuchus skull, with published reconstructions differing greatly.
facts.quote: Two reconstructions of the skull of Mekosuchus have been published, differing greatly from one another.

facts.statement: M. inexpectatus has been estimated to reach a length of approximately 2 meters.
facts.quote: M. inexpectatus for instance has been estimated to have reached a length of approximately 2 m by Balouet

facts.statement: Holt and colleagues estimate that members of the genus Mekosuchus are around 1 meter in length.
facts.quote: Holt and colleagues estimate members of Mekosuchus to be around 1 m in length.

facts.statement: Mekosuchus was classified as a Eusuchian based on its choanae and procoelous vertebrae and placed in the family Mekosuchidae.
facts.quote: They ultimately determined that Mekosuchus was a Eusuchian based on the choanae and the procoelous vertebrae, and placed it in the monotypic family Mekosuchidae

facts.statement: The family originally named Mekosuchidae is now referred to as Mekosuchinae after research placed other Australasian taxa within it.
facts.quote: Since then, research on Australasian crocodilians has placed a wide range of other taxa in the family, which is now referred to by the name Mekosuchinae.

facts.statement: Willis (1997) suggested a close link between Mekosuchus and Trilophosuchus, with Quinkana as their sister taxon.
facts.quote: Willis (1997) suggests a close link between Mekosuchus and Trilophosuchus, with Quinkana as their sister taxon

facts.statement: A 2018 study by Lee & Yates using morphological, molecular, and stratigraphic data recovered phylogenetic results broadly similar to previous analyses.
facts.quote: A 2018 tip dating study by Lee & Yates using a combination of morphological, molecular (DNA sequencing), and stratigraphic (fossil age) data recovered broadly similar results

facts.statement: Fossil evidence indicates that Mekosuchus originated on mainland Australia, but its dispersal throughout the South Pacific is poorly understood.
facts.quote: While fossil evidence shows that Mekosuchus originated on mainland Australia, little is known about how it dispersed throughout the South Pacific.

facts.statement: M. inexpectatus is known exclusively from New Caledonia, making it the geographically closest mekosuchine to mainland Australia.
facts.quote: This species is known exclusively from New Caledonia, which makes it the closest geographically to mainland Australia.

facts.statement: Mead and colleagues identify the Oligocene as the earliest possible date for dispersal, though a more recent Quaternary dispersal is considered more likely.
facts.quote: Mead and colleagues name the Oligocene as the earliest possible date, though an even more recent Quaternary dispersal is deemed more likely.

facts.statement: It is debated whether mekosuchines actively swam between landmasses or drifted using natural rafts to disperse.
facts.quote: it is possible that they could have actively swam between landmasses or drifted with the use of natural rafts

facts.statement: Mekosuchus had a high, vertical skull shape adapted for terrestrial life rather than the flattened shape of semi-aquatic crocodilians.
facts.quote: The skull is altirostral, similar to extinct terrestrial forms like Notosuchians and members of the Planocraniidae, while semi-aquatic crocodilians typically have flattened platyrostral skulls

facts.statement: The nostrils and eyes of Mekosuchus were positioned on the front and sides of the skull, indicating it was not built for an aquatic lifestyle.
facts.quote: Rather than opening towards the top of the skull, which would allow the animal to breathe while remaining largely submerged, the nares open towards the front of the skull, and the eyes are similarly directed towards the sides, not the top

facts.statement: In 1995, Paul Willis hypothesized that Mekosuchus might have been arboreal and filled a niche similar to modern monitor lizards.
facts.quote: In 1995 Australian paleontologist Paul Willis informally suggested that animals like Mekosuchines may have filled a niche equivalent to modern monitor lizards, even going as far as to suggest arboreal (climbing) habits

facts.statement: Recent research has dismissed the idea that Mekosuchus was an exceptional climber because monitor lizards were already present in Australia and the animal's toe bones did not differ significantly from other crocodilians.
facts.quote: However, this idea has been dismissed by more recent research, as monitor lizards had been present in Australia for longer than assumed by Willis, while analysis of mekosuchine toe bones showed no significant differences to those of other crocodilians and thus not supporting the notion that they were exceptional climbers

facts.statement: Mekosuchus whitehunterensis is believed to have possessed strong neck muscles used for ripping flesh from carcasses.
facts.quote: The strong neck musculature inferred for Mekosuchus whitehunterensis has been interpreted as being an adaptation for ripping chunks of flesh from carcasses

facts.statement: Due to its small size, Mekosuchus likely used headshaking rather than the death roll maneuver to feed, as the latter is less effective in animals smaller than 3-4 meters.
facts.quote: It is noted that the small size of Mekosuchus would render the death roll maneuver less effective than in species with a body length between 3-4 m long, whereas headshaking is favored by small animals like juveniles

facts.statement: Mekosuchus inexpectatus possessed specialized back teeth adapted for cracking hard-shelled invertebrates like molluscs, crustaceans, and insects, unlike the bladed teeth of mainland species.
facts.quote: Unlike the bladed teeth of the mainland species, Mekosuchus inexpectatus had specialized back teeth more suited for cracking hard-shelled invertebrates such as molluscs, crustaceans and insects

facts.statement: Holt and colleagues suggest that Mekosuchus inexpectatus may have lived a lifestyle similar to modern dwarf crocodiles or dwarf caimans.
facts.quote: Based on newer material and the previously noted similarities between Mekosuchus and modern dwarf crocodiles, Holt and colleagues suggest that M. inexpectatus could have possibly lived a similar lifestyle to the modern dwarf crocodiles (Osteolaemus spp.) or dwarf caimans (Paleosuchus spp.)

facts.statement: Holt and colleagues hypothesize that Mekosuchus inexpectatus inhabited slow-moving streams in New Caledonia rainforests and foraged at night near water and on land.
facts.quote: According to their hypothesis, M. inexpectatus may have inhabited small, slow moving streams in the rainforests of New Caledonia and foraged at night near the waters edge and on land

facts.statement: The link between human arrival and Mekosuchus extinction is disputed; Anderson and colleagues note that most Mekosuchus inexpectatus remains predate human settlement in New Caledonia.
facts.quote: However, this idea is not universally accepted and has been disputed by other researchers. Anderson and colleagues for instance note that in the case of Mekosuchus inexpectatus, most remains were deposited prior to human settlement of New Caledonia, with only a single mandible overlapping with human presence

facts.statement: Mekosuchus resembled dwarf caimans and crocodiles in size and ecology, making them potentially easier prey for humans than larger continental crocodilians.
facts.quote: Size and inferred ecology of Mekosuchus somewhat resemble todays species of dwarf caimans and dwarf crocodiles, both of which are exploited by humans as a food source and would pose no significant threat to would-be hunters even once they've reached maturity, making them easier prey than their contemporary continental cousins

facts.quote: genus_authority: Balouet & Buffetaut, 1987

facts.statement: The most recent species, M. kalpokasi, was named in 2002 based on fragmentary remains from an archaeological site in Vanuatu.

facts.statement: Fossils from Pindai Caves appear younger, with dates as recent as 1,720 years according to Balouet and Buffetaut.
facts.quote: los fósiles de la Cuevas de Pindai Caves parecen ser más jóvenes, dando resultados tan cercanos cómo 1,720 años según Balouet y Buffetaut

facts.statement: Over 300 specimens have been found at Pindai, but most remain undescribed.
facts.quote: Se han encontrado más de 300 en Pindai , pero la gran mayoría de estos permanecen indescritos

facts.statement: M. kalpokasi from Efate Island, Vanuatu, dates to between 3,200 and 2,706 years ago.
facts.quote: M. kalpokasi, de la isla de Éfaté de Vanuatu rondano una antigüedad entre 3,200 y 2,706 años

facts.statement: The specific name kalpokasi honors Donald Kalpokas, the Prime Minister of Vanuatu during the discovery.
facts.quote: El nombre específico viene del primer ministro de Vanuatu durante el descubrimiento, Donald Kalpokas

facts.statement: M. sanderi, the second youngest Australian species, lived in the early Miocene of Queensland and was named by Willis based on two maxillae and cranial fragments from the Ringtail site (Faunal Zone C) at Riversleigh.
facts.quote: M. sanderi es la segunda y más joven especie de Mekosuchus australiania, viviendo en el Mioceno temprano de Queensland. Fue nombrada por Willis basándose en dos maxilares y varios fragmentos craneales, todos con origen del sitio Ringtail (Zona faunal C) de Riversleigh

facts.statement: M. whitehunterensis is the oldest species in the genus, living from the late Oligocene to the early Miocene in Queensland.
facts.quote: M. whitehunterensis esla especie más antigua del género, viviendo desde el Oligoceno tardío al Mioceno temprano de Queensland

facts.statement: The specific name whitehunterensis refers to the White Hunter site, which yielded the first fossils.
facts.quote: El nombre específico hace referencia al Sitio White Hunter,la localidad que originó los primeros fósiles

facts.statement: Mekosuchus is an extinct genus of Australasian crocodiles belonging to the subfamily Mekosuchinae.
facts.quote: Mekosuchus es un género extinto de cocodrilos australasianos de la subfamilia Mekosuchinae

facts.statement: Due to the strange anatomy of the remains, they were originally thought to be an early eusuchian and classified under their own family, Mekosuchidae.
facts.quote: Debido a la extraña anatomía de los restos, originalmente pensaron que se trataba de un eusuquio temprano (considerado por entonces como un suborden de Crocodilia) y lo clasificaron bajo su propia familia, Mekosuchidae

facts.statement: Currently, four species of Mekosuchus are recognized: M. inexpectatus, M. whitehunterensis, M. sanderi, and M. kalpokasi, all known from fragmentary fossils.
facts.quote: Actualmente se reconocen cuatro especies, M. inexpectatus, M. whitehunterensis, M. sanderi y M. kalpokasi, todas conocidas de fósiles fragmentarios

facts.statement: Holt and colleagues believe the poor condition of M. kalpokasi remains might indicate it was a single species synonymous with M. inexpectatus.
facts.quote: Holt y colegas creen que esto pudiera indicar que se trataban de una sola especie, sininimizándola con M. inexpectatus

facts.statement: While archaeological remains suggest coexistence with humans, the ages of these materials are disputed, with some authors suggesting a Pleistocene origin.
facts.quote: Si bein los restos en yacimientos arqueológicos indican que coexistieron con humanos, las edades de estos materiales se disputa, con autores sugiriendo un origen en el Pleistoceno

facts.statement: Researchers originally classified Mekosuchus as a eusuchian based on its coanas and procoelous vertebrae, establishing the monotypic family Mekosuchidae.
facts.quote: Acabaron determinando que Mekosuchus fue un eusuquio basándose en las coanas y las vértebras procelosas, irguieron la familia monotípica Mekosuchidae

facts.statement: Later analyses of Australian crocodilians placed many taxa within the family under the new name Mekosuchinae.
facts.quote: Desde entonces, análisis de crocodilos australianos ha colocado un gran número de taxones dentro de la familia, bajo el nuevo nombre de Mekosuchinae

facts.statement: Willis (1997) suggested a close relationship between Mekosuchus and Trilophosuchus, with Quinkana as its sister taxon.
facts.quote: Willis (1997) sugiere una relación estrecha entre Mekosuchus and Trilophosuchus, con Quinkana como su taxón hermano

facts.statement: Mead et al. (2002) placed Mekosuchus, Quinkana, and the unnamed Volia as sisters of Trilophosuchus within the clade Mekosuchini.

facts.statement: A 2018 analysis by Lee and Yates recovered similar relationships but found different results for the Mekosuchini clade.
facts.quote: Un análisis de ADN molecular, morfológico y estratográfico de 2018 por Lee y Yates recuperó relaciones similares, aunque las de Mekosuchini salieron diferentes

facts.statement: The most recent analysis by Ristevski et al. in 2023 focused not only on mekosuchines but on all Australasian crocodylomorphs in general.
facts.quote: El análisis más reciente, de Ristevski et al. en 2023 puso mayor foco no sólo en los mekosuquinos sino todos los crocodilomorfos australasiáticos en general

facts.statement: These results showed that most mekosuchines belonged to Mekosuchini, which was split into two clades separating larger/continental forms from smaller/insular ones.
facts.quote: Estos resultaron con la mayoría de mekosuquinos perteneciendo a Mekosuchini, que a su vez fue separado en dos clados, separando las formas mayores y/o continentales de las menores y/o insulares

facts.statement: Notably, "Baru" huberi was recovered as the most basal member of this group, while Quinkana joined the larger continental forms.
facts.quote: Notablemente, "Baru" huberi fue recuperado como el miembro más basal de este grupo, mientras que Quinkana se unió a aquellos más grandes continentales

facts.statement: The rest deviates considerably from traditional Mekosuchinae compositions, with members of Kambara and Australosuchus belonging to both other parts of Crocodylia and Mekosuchinae.
facts.quote: El resto deriva considerablemente de composiciones tradicionales de Mekosuchinae, con miembros de Kambara y Australosuchus perteneciendo tanto a otras partes de Crocodylia como a Mekosuchinae

facts.statement: Regardless of the relationship between Mekosuchinae and Orientalosuchina, the closest relatives of Mekosuchus remain the same, generally recovering the same clade of small animals composed of "Baru" huberi, Volia, Trilophosuchus, and Mekosuchus.
facts.quote: Sin importar la relación entre Mekosuchinae y Orientalosuchina, tlos parientes más cercanos de Mekosuchus son los mismos, generalmente recuperando el mismo clado de animales pequeños compuesto de "Baru" huberi, Volia, Trilophosuchus y Mekosuchus

facts.statement: The genus Mekosuchus was named by Balouet and Buffetaut in 1987.
facts.quote: PBDB name: Mekosuchus (genus), Balouet and Buffetaut 1987

facts.statement: Mekosuchus lived from the Chattian to the Holocene, spanning from 27.3 to 0 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Chattian to Holocene (27.3 to 0 million years ago)

facts.statement: M. inexpectatus is believed to have had the longest temporal range of the three, originating around 4,000 years ago.
facts.quote: Se cree que M. inexpectatus tuvo el mayor rango temporal de los tres, originando hará 4,000 años

facts.statement: Since mekosuchines appeared in the Eocene, Mead and colleagues suggest that continental drift and separation could not have affected their appearance in the South Pacific.
facts.quote: Como los mekosuquinos aparecieron en el Eoceno, Mead y colaboradores sugieren que la deriva continental y separación no pudieron tener efecto en su aparición en el Pacífico Sur

facts.statement: Although it is not certain if mekosuchines possessed adaptations or tolerance for saltwater like modern crocodiles, it remains possible they swam directly between islands or arrived via natural rafts.

facts.statement: Both processes could have taken advantage of low sea levels in the late Cenozoic, reducing the distance between islands and at times joining island chains into one.

facts.statement: Mead and colleagues believe the dispersal began in the Oligocene, although some defend the Quaternary as a more probable date.
facts.quote: Mead y colaboradores creen que comenzó en el Oligoceno, aunque hay quienes defienden el Cuaternario como una fecha más probable
